en: Itivuttaka 26: Ekakanipāta, Third Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: "Monks, there is this one thing which, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. What is that one thing? It is unwholesome greed (*lobha*). This is the one thing, monks, which, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Blessed One: "How is it, venerable sir, that unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune? "Monk, suppose a man were to take a small amount of salt and throw it into a small cup of water. What do you think, monk? Would that small cup of water become salty and undrinkable because of that small amount of salt? "Yes, venerable sir. "But what if, monk, that same man were to take that same small amount of salt and throw it into the great ocean? What do you think, monk? Would that great ocean become salty and undrinkable because of that small amount of salt? "No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because the great ocean is deep, vast, and immeasurable. "In the same way, monk, there are these five bases for the origination of craving. What five? Form, sound, odor, taste, and tactile object. These, monk, are the five bases for the origination of craving. If, monk, a bhikkhu delights in form, finds pleasure in form, and finds gratification in form, then unwholesome greed will arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, when it has arisen, will bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. If, monk, a bhikkhu delights in sound... delights in odor... delights in taste... delights in tactile objects, finds pleasure in them, and finds gratification in them, then unwholesome greed will arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, when it has arisen, will bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. But if, monk, a bhikkhu does not delight in form, does not find pleasure in form, and does not find gratification in form, then unwholesome greed will not arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, not having arisen, will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. If, monk, a bhikkhu does not delight in sound... does not delight in odor... does not delight in taste... does not delight in tactile objects, does not find pleasure in them, and does not find gratification in them, then unwholesome greed will not arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, not having arisen, will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Just as, monk, if a man were to take that same small amount of salt and throw it into the great ocean, it would not make the great ocean salty and undrinkable; for what reason? Because the great ocean is deep, vast, and immeasurable—so too, monk, if a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained regarding these five bases for the origination of craving, then even if unwholesome greed should arise in him, it will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, that monk approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Just now, friend Ānanda, I approached the Blessed One and asked him: 'How is it, venerable sir, that unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune? And the Venerable Ānanda explained to me in detail how unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. "It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well the Venerable Ānanda has stated this. For indeed, friend, the Blessed One has declared: 'Monks, there is this one thing which, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. What is that one thing? It is unwholesome greed. And the Venerable Ānanda has explained in detail how unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Blessed One: "How is it, venerable sir, that unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune? "Monk, suppose a man were to take a small amount of salt and throw it into a small cup of water. What do you think, monk? Would that small cup of water become salty and undrinkable because of that small amount of salt? "Yes, venerable sir. "But what if, monk, that same man were to take that same small amount of salt and throw it into the great ocean? What do you think, monk? Would that great ocean become salty and undrinkable because of that small amount of salt? "No, venerable sir. For what reason? Because the great ocean is deep, vast, and immeasurable. "In the same way, monk, there are these five bases for the origination of craving. What five? Form, sound, odor, taste, and tactile object. These, monk, are the five bases for the origination of craving. If, monk, a bhikkhu delights in form, finds pleasure in form, and finds gratification in form, then unwholesome greed will arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, when it has arisen, will bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. If, monk, a bhikkhu delights in sound... delights in odor... delights in taste... delights in tactile objects, finds pleasure in them, and finds gratification in them, then unwholesome greed will arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, when it has arisen, will bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. But if, monk, a bhikkhu does not delight in form, does not find pleasure in form, and does not find gratification in form, then unwholesome greed will not arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, not having arisen, will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. If, monk, a bhikkhu does not delight in sound... does not delight in odor... does not delight in taste... does not delight in tactile objects, does not find pleasure in them, and does not find gratification in them, then unwholesome greed will not arise in him, and that unwholesome greed, not having arisen, will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Just as, monk, if a man were to take that same small amount of salt and throw it into the great ocean, it would not make the great ocean salty and undrinkable; for what reason? Because the great ocean is deep, vast, and immeasurable—so too, monk, if a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained regarding these five bases for the origination of craving, then even if unwholesome greed should arise in him, it will not bring about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, that monk approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, that monk said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Just now, friend Ānanda, I approached the Blessed One and asked him: 'How is it, venerable sir, that unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune? And the Venerable Ānanda explained to me in detail how unwholesome greed, when it arises in a person, brings about his downfall, his ruin, and his misfortune. "It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend!
The Discourse on Giving.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, if beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of miserliness persist, taking hold of their minds."
“Even their very last morsel, their very last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, were there others to receive it.
But because beings do not know the ripening of the fruit of giving and sharing as I know it, they eat without having given; and the stain of stinginess persists, taking possession of their minds.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
In this connection, it is said:
“If beings would understand in the way described by the Great Seer;”
How the ripening of sharing becomes so very fruitful—
having removed the stain of stinginess.
With a serene mind,
one should give at the proper time to the Noble Ones,
where what is given bears great fruit.
Having given much food as an offering to those worthy of offerings,
when one passes away from this human state,
The donors go to heaven;
having gone there to heaven,
they rejoice, obtaining whatever they desire.
“Those who are not stingy experience the result of sharing.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The sixth.
